analysis_trace: Trial NCT06325709 is a Phase 1/2 single-arm study evaluating base-edited autologous CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells for X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) with the specific CYBB c.676C>T mutation.
The intervention uses cytosine base editing to correct the mutation, with busulfan conditioning (target AUC 65,000 ng/mL x hr), alemtuzumab (Campath) and sirolimus immunomodulation.

Evidence sources: Retrieved literature on gene therapy for CGD, base editing in hematopoietic stem cells, and lentiviral gene therapy precedents. Key references include 2024 Sci Transl Med on high-fidelity base editing for CGD (PMID 39413163), 2020 Nat Med on lentiviral gene therapy for X-CGD (PMID 31988463), and 2024 review on gene therapy for inborn errors of immunity.

Primary safety endpoint (primary-0): Based on gene therapy HSCT experience, serious adverse events are expected in 20-40% of patients related to busulfan conditioning and immunosuppression. Base editing-specific safety concerns include off-target effects and chromosomal abnormalities, though base editing has lower risk than nuclease editing.

Primary efficacy endpoint (primary-1): Historical lentiviral gene therapy for X-CGD achieved >10% oxidase-positive granulocytes in most patients. Base editing preclinical data showed efficient correction. Predict 70-80% of patients will achieve ≥10% oxidase-positive granulocytes at 12 months.

Secondary endpoints: gp91 expression (secondary-0) and edited myeloid cells (secondary-1) expected to correlate with oxidase-positive rates. gp91phox protein restoration (secondary-2) and DHR+ cells (secondary-3) are mechanistic correlates of functional NADPH oxidase restoration.

Clinical efficacy (secondary-4): Infection frequency reduction expected but requires longer follow-up. Gene correction stability (secondary-5): Base editing creates precise edits without double-strand breaks, predicting stable correction in hematopoietic stem cells.
Evidence gaps: No published clinical results from this specific trial; base editing in CGD is first-in-human; long-term durability unknown.
Population: Adult males (≥18 years) with confirmed CYBB c.676C>T mutation, history of serious infections, clinically stable for conditioning.
Key risks: Conditioning toxicity, graft failure, insufficient engraftment of edited cells, immune response to gp91phox, insertional oncogenesis (lower risk with base editing than viral vectors).

analysis_trace: Trial NCT06325709 is a Phase 1/2 single-arm study evaluating base-edited autologous CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells for X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) with the specific CYBB c.676C>T mutation.
The intervention uses cytosine base editing to correct the mutation, with busulfan conditioning (target AUC 65,000 ng/mL x hr), alemtuzumab (Campath) and sirolimus immunomodulation.

Evidence sources: Retrieved literature on gene therapy for CGD, base editing in hematopoietic stem cells, and lentiviral gene therapy precedents. Key references include 2024 Sci Transl Med on high-fidelity base editing for CGD (PMID 39413163), 2020 Nat Med on lentiviral gene therapy for X-CGD (PMID 31988463), and 2024 review on gene therapy for inborn errors of immunity.

Primary safety endpoint (primary-0): Based on gene therapy HSCT experience, serious adverse events are expected in 20-40% of patients related to busulfan conditioning and immunosuppression. Base editing-specific safety concerns include off-target effects and chromosomal abnormalities, though base editing has lower risk than nuclease editing.

Primary efficacy endpoint (primary-1): Historical lentiviral gene therapy for X-CGD achieved >10% oxidase-positive granulocytes in most patients. Base editing preclinical data showed efficient correction. Predict 70-80% of patients will achieve ≥10% oxidase-positive granulocytes at 12 months.

Secondary endpoints: gp91 expression (secondary-0) and edited myeloid cells (secondary-1) expected to correlate with oxidase-positive rates. gp91phox protein restoration (secondary-2) and DHR+ cells (secondary-3) are mechanistic correlates of functional NADPH oxidase restoration.

Clinical efficacy (secondary-4): Infection frequency reduction expected but requires longer follow-up. Gene correction stability (secondary-5): Base editing creates precise edits without double-strand breaks, predicting stable correction in hematopoietic stem cells.
Evidence gaps: No published clinical results from this specific trial; base editing in CGD is first-in-human; long-term durability unknown.
Population: Adult males (≥18 years) with confirmed CYBB c.676C>T mutation, history of serious infections, clinically stable for conditioning.
Key risks: Conditioning toxicity, graft failure, insufficient engraftment of edited cells, immune response to gp91phox, insertional oncogenesis (lower risk with base editing than viral vectors).

analysis_trace.indication: X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (X-CGD), a rare primary immunodeficiency caused by CYBB mutations affecting gp91phox and NADPH oxidase activity.
analysis_trace.patient_population: Adult males (18-75 years) with confirmed CYBB c.676C>T mutation, history of serious infections, clinically stable for conditioning. N=15 estimated.
analysis_trace.target_mechanism: ABE8e-SpRY adenine base editor corrects the C>T mutation at position c.676 in CYBB, restoring endogenous gp91phox expression without double-strand breaks. Preclinical data showed up to 70% correction efficiency in HSPCs.
analysis_trace.endpoint_interpretation: Primary-0: Safety endpoint (AEs/SAEs) over 2 years. Primary-1: Efficacy threshold >=10% oxidase-positive granulocytes at 12 months. Secondaries: gp91 expression, edited myeloid cells, DHR+ cells, infection frequency, allele stability.
analysis_trace.safety_analysis: Busulfan conditioning (12 mg/kg) carries risks of mucositis, cytopenias, infection. Immunosuppression with alemtuzumab and sirolimus adds infection risk. Base editing off-target profile appears favorable per preclinical data.
analysis_trace.key_risks: 1) Engraftment failure or poor durability; 2) Insufficient editing efficiency to reach 10% threshold; 3) Busulfan toxicity; 4) Immune response to edited cells; 5) Graft loss (observed in 3/19 prior lentiviral CGD patients).
analysis_trace.evidence_to_prediction: Preclinical study (Sci Transl Med 2024) demonstrated 70% correction efficiency for CYBB c.676C>T in HSPCs, with stable edited alleles post-transplant in mice. Prior lentiviral GT (Nat Med 2020) achieved 16-46% oxidase-positive neutrophils in 6/7 survivors at 12 months. Base editing avoids vector insertional risk and should achieve comparable or better engraftment with endogenous regulation.
analysis_trace.coverage_gaps: No published clinical results for this specific trial as of cutoff. Phase 1/2 design with small sample (n=15) limits precision. Long-term durability (>2 years) uncertain. No direct comparative data for base editing vs lentiviral GT in humans.

{"url": "https://crisprmedicinenews.com/clinical-trial/chronic-granulomatous-disease-cgd-nct06325709/", "content_type": "text/html; charset=utf-8", "text": "Logo mobilemenu close CMN Live Home Clinical Trials CMN DB 2.0 CRISPRMED CRISPRMED24 CRISPRMED25 CRISPRMED26 WDC CRISPRMED26 Contest CRISPRMED26 Conference Kit CRISPRMED27 CRISPRMED Website Policies EGMEDC CMN Intelligence Webinars Advertising WDC About search Selfservice | Subscriberlogin Logout Prime Editors Base Editors Delivery Safety Off-target Microbiome CAR-T TIL Rare Diseases Trials Explainers CMN Weekly CARBON ** The new CMN Global Trials Database 2.0 is now available ** Disease: Chronic Granulomatous Disease, CGD, (NCT06325709) Disease info: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) results in immune system dysfunction, leading to immunodeficiency. This may cause recurring bacterial and fungal infections and inflammation in various parts of the body. Symptoms usually start in childhood, though some may not appear until later in life. Individuals with CGD often experience serious bacterial or fungal infections every few years, with the lungs being the most common site of infection, often leading to pneumonia. Exposure to certain organic materials can trigger fungal pneumonia. Other areas commonly affected include the skin, liver, and lymph nodes. In some cases, CGD can lead to autoimmune disorders, where the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues. Repeated infections and inflammation can shorten life expectancy, but with treatment, most people with CGD can live into their mid- to late adulthood. Most cases of CGD are caused by mutations in five genes,  CYBA , CYBB , NCF1 , NCF2 , CYBC1 , or NCF4 , which each encode a subunit of the NADPH oxidase enzyme complex that plays a crucial role in immune function. CGD is categorised into five types, distinguished by the associated genetic variant. A mutation in the CYBB gene (Xp21.1) is found in approximately 65% of cases in North America and Western Europe. The resulting deficiency in the NADPH oxidase enzyme complex leads to decreased production of reactive oxygen species (used by phagocytes to kill bacteria and fungi). Consequently, individuals with CGD are prone to infections and excessive inflammation. Some cases of CGD have unknown genetic causes.  CGD presents with a range of symptoms affecting various organ systems. Common manifestations include severe and recurrent infections, often caused by specific pathogens such as  Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus spp. Additionally, patients may develop granulomatous lesions, primarily affecting the lungs, lymph nodes, gastrointestinal tract, and liver. Up to half of patients may experience symptoms such as diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and failure to thrive. Common complications can include pneumonia, abscesses, cellulitis, adenitis, and osteomyelitis. Mycobacterial diseases are typically limited to tuberculosis or disseminated Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) infections, while invasive fungal infections are frequent. Dysregulated inflammation and granuloma formation can lead to various complications, including chorioretinal lesions, gastric outlet obstruction, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and wound complications. Most female carriers of CGD show no symptoms unless a significant portion of their neutrophils are dysfunctional. Some individuals with CGD may develop autoimmune disorders such as discoid lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome. Frequency: CGD is estimated to occur in 1 in 200,000 to 250,000 people worldwide. Official title: Phase 1/2 Trial of Base Editing for Mutation Repair in Hematopoietic Stem & Progenitor Cells for X-linked Chronic Granulomatous Disease Who: Sponsor: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Partners: Locations: United States, Maryland National Institutes of Health Clinical Center, Bethesda, Maryland, United States, 20892 Study start: Apr. 10, 2024 Enrollment: 10 participants Gene editing method: CRISPR-Cas9 Type of edit: Base edit Gene: Cytochrome B Beta (CYBB) Delivery method: Lentivirus (LV) vector - Ex-vivo Trial link: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06325709 Indicator Indicator IND Enabling Pre-clinical Phase I Safety Phase II Safety and Dosing Phase III Safety and Efficacy Status: Active recruiting Description Open-label, phase 1/2 trial to determine the safety, and efficacy of a single infusion of base-edited (BE) autologous hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) for treatment of X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (X-CGD). Base editing is performed to repair CYBB missense gene mutations (eg, CYBB c.676C>T). The study hypotheses are that 1) base editing can efficiently repair gene mutations in HSPCs; and 2) BE HSPCs can engraft and differentiate into functional phagocytes with restored nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase activity. During the initial development phase each study participant will undergo apheresis for CD34+ HSPC collection for the development and validation of a mutation-specific BE system. During the treatment phase, participants will receive a one-time infusion of the BE autologous HSPC Investigational Medicinal Product (IMP) after busulfan (total 12 mg/kg) conditioning. Participants will have follow-up evaluations at months 3, 6, 12, 18, and 24, and yearly thereafter until 5 years after treatment. Key study assessments include adverse event (AE) assessment, blood laboratory evaluations of functional protein made from the target gene (CYBB, encodes for gp91^phox), and deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequencing to identify rates of gene repair and off-target mutation. The final study follow-up under this protocol will be at 5 years, but long-term follow-up under a separate NIH protocol will continue annually to 15 years after treatment. The applicability of base editors (BEs) to correct mutations that cause X-CGD is constrained by the requirement of Clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-associated (Cas) enzymes to recognize specific protospacer adjacent motifs (PAMs). Our recently engineered PAMless Cas enzyme, SpRY, can overcome the PAM limitation. However, the efficiency, specificity, and applicability of SpRY-based BEs to correct mutations in human hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPCs) has not been thoroughly examined. Here we demonstrated that the adenine base editor ABE8e-SpRY can access a range of target sites in HSPCs to correct mutations causative of X-CGD. For the prototypical X-CGD mutation CYBB c.676C>T, ABE8e-SpRY achieved up to 70% correction, reaching efficiencies greater than 3.5 times higher than previous CRISPR nuclease and donor template approaches. We profiled potential off-target DNA edits, transcriptome-wide RNA edits, and chromosomal perturbations in base-edited HSPCs, which together revealed minimal off-target or bystander edits. Edited alleles persisted following transplantation of base-edited HSPCs into immunodeficient mice. Altogether, these investigational new drug (IND)-enabling studies demonstrated efficient and precise correction of an X-CGD mutation with PAMless BEs, supporting a first-in-human clinical trial ( NCT06325709 ) and providing a potential blueprint for treatment of other IEI mutations. Introduction Ex vivo hematopoietic stem and progenitor stem cell (HSPC) gene therapy using self-inactivating lentiviral vectors (LVs) have provided clinical benefit for treatment of multiple inborn errors of immunity (IEI), including Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD), X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID), ADA-deficient SCID, and Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome ( 1 – 4 ). However, potential vector insertional oncogenesis remains a concern as observed in cerebral adrenoleukodystrophy ( 5 ), or aberrant fusion transcripts such as high mobility group AT-hook 2 ( HMGA2) + clonal expansion in X-SCID ( 6 ) and β-thalassemia ( 7 ). LV-mediated constitutive gene over-expression and the lack of physiological regulation are also unacceptable for many IEIs due to mutations in tightly-regulated genes, such as CD40L-deficient hyper-IgM syndrome ( 8 , 9 ). Thus, there is a major unmet need for more efficient and safer gene therapies for IEIs. Recent progress in the development of genome editing technologies may help solve these key challenges. Next-generation CRISPR-Cas-based genome editing approaches permit user-specifiable genetic alterations to alter cellular function efficiently in HSPCs and engineered T cells ( 10 – 13 ). By enabling the correction of the underlying genetic mutations, rather than overexpressing a corrective transgene, genome editing approaches could offer an improved safety profile with broad applicability for many IEIs. CGD is an inherited disorder that is typically caused by a defective phagocyte nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH) oxidase complex, resulting in reduced bactericidal reactive oxidative species for host defense. Patients with CGD experience recurrent invasive infections, hyperinflammation and inflammatory bowel disease ( 14 – 16 ), with increased morbidity and early mortality from infection rates of 0.3/year, despite antimicrobial prophylaxis ( 15 ). Ex vivo gene therapy for X-linked CGD (X-CGD) to restore canonical gp91 phox protein expression using lentiviral vector-transduced autologous HSPCs has treated 19 patients to date, three of whom have lost their grafts for reasons as yet unclear ( 2 ). Peripheral blood granulocytes from treated patients express gp91 phox at about 1/3 of normal donor amounts due to a relatively weak chimeric promoter ( 2 , 17 ). Permanent semi-random vector insertion, the use of weak exogenous promoter to reduce risks of transactivating nearby oncogenes, and the lack of physiological regulation are all issues with this previous approach that provide rationale to explore other approaches including targeted genome editing. We recently demonstrated that genome editing could be applied to restore endogenous gp91 phox expression at physiological amounts ( 17 ). To correct the CYBB c.676C>T mutation on the X chromosome, we utilized a CRISPR-Cas9 nuclease to create a targeted DNA double-strand break (DSB) with subsequent repair via homology-directed repair (HDR) using a short 100-nt DNA donor. However, relatively inefficient HDR and adverse effects of Cas9 induced DSBs have been reported, including activation of the DNA damage response, unwanted insertion or deletion mutations at the on-target site, large chromosomal deletions, translocations, chromothripsis, and others ( 18 – 24 ). Next-generation genome editing technologies including base editors (BEs) overcome some of these concerns by correcting genetic mutations without intentionally introducing DSBs ( 25 )( 26 – 28 ). BEs are comprised of a Cas9 nickase fused to a DNA deaminase domain, which initiates the installation of C-to-T or A-to-G genome edits via cytidine base editors (CBE) or adenine base editors (ABE) respectively). A guide RNA (gRNA) is expressed in trans to direct the BE to a target site that is flanked by a protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM). However, the deaminase domain of BEs can typically only act within a short ‘edit window’ of the target site, restricting edit efficiency and flexibility ( 29 , 30 ). The edit window is typically nucleotides 4–9 of the spacer region of the target ( 29 ), which means that base edits are possible at a fixed distance from PAM of the target site. Thus, PAM availability is one of the major determinants of which regions of the genome are accessible for base editing. The conventional PAM for Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) is NGG, where ‘N’ is any nucleotide ( 31 – 33 ). For base editing approaches to correct point mutations, there is often not an NGG PAM available in the correct position of the target site to appropriately place the edit window of the BE over the edit of interest. We report initial results of nine severely affected X-linked CGD (X-CGD) patients who received ex vivo autologous CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell-based lentiviral gene therapy following myeloablative conditioning in first-in-man studies (Trial registry numbers: NCT02234934 , NCT01855685 ). Primary objectives were to assess safety and evaluate efficacy and stability of biochemical and functional reconstitution in the progeny of engrafted cells at 12 months. The secondary objectives included the evaluation of augmented immunity against bacterial and fungal infection, and assessment of hematopoietic stem cell transduction and engraftment. Two enrolled patients died within 3 months of treatment from pre-existing comorbidities. At 12 months, six of the seven surviving patients demonstrated stable vector copy number (0.4–1.8 copies/neutrophil) and persistence of 16–46% oxidase-positive neutrophils. There was no molecular evidence of clonal dysregulation or of transgene silencing. Surviving patients have had no new CGD-related infections, and six have been able to discontinue CGD-related antibiotic prophylaxis. The primary objective was met in 6 of the 9 patients at 12 months follow-up suggesting that autologous gene therapy is a promising approach for CGD patients. Introduction X-CGD is caused by mutations in CYBB encoding the gp91phox subunit of the phagocyte nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH)-oxidase (NOX2). Patients are susceptible to recurrent life-threatening infections, impacting their quality of life and life-expectancy. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) can be curative, and recent advances have improved the results from this treatment considerably 3 , 4 . Clinical trials of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) gene therapy were first initiated with gammaretroviral (γ-RV) vectors. 5 , 6 . However, clonal expansion of gene-corrected cells mediated by potent enhancer elements in the γ-RV long-terminal repeats (LTRs) 5 , 7 , eventually lead to leukoproliferative complications. In addition, CpG dinucleotide promoter methylation lead to silencing of transgene expression 7 . To retain the efficacy of gene therapy for X-CGD, but minimize mutagenic risk, a self-inactivating lentiviral vector called G1XCGD was developed ( Fig. 1a , full sequence shown in Extended Data 1 ). To enhance the safety of this vector, a novel chimeric internal promoter was used to preferentially drive gp91phox expression at high levels in phagocytes 8 , 9 . Complementary clinical studies were initiated, including a multicenter trial in the USA, a UK study and compassionate-use program with nearly identical clinical protocols, eligibility criteria, myeloablative conditioning, stem cell product manufacturing methods, vector batches, and post-transplant analyses. analysis_trace.trial_identification: NCT06325709 is a Phase 1/2 open-label single-arm trial of base-edited autologous HSPCs for X-linked CGD (CYBB c.676C>T mutation). Sponsor: NIAID. Status: RECRUITING. Expected completion: 2032.
analysis_trace.indication: X-linked chronic granulomatous disease (X-CGD), a rare primary immunodeficiency caused by CYBB mutations affecting gp91phox and NADPH oxidase activity.
analysis_trace.patient_population: Adult males (18-75 years) with confirmed CYBB c.676C>T mutation, history of serious infections, clinically stable for conditioning. N=15 estimated.
analysis_trace.target_mechanism: ABE8e-SpRY adenine base editor corrects the C>T mutation at position c.676 in CYBB, restoring endogenous gp91phox expression without double-strand breaks. Preclinical data showed up to 70% correction efficiency in HSPCs.
analysis_trace.endpoint_interpretation: Primary-0: Safety endpoint (AEs/SAEs) over 2 years. Primary-1: Efficacy threshold >=10% oxidase-positive granulocytes at 12 months. Secondaries: gp91 expression, edited myeloid cells, DHR+ cells, infection frequency, allele stability.
analysis_trace.safety_analysis: Busulfan conditioning (12 mg/kg) carries risks of mucositis, cytopenias, infection. Immunosuppression with alemtuzumab and sirolimus adds infection risk. Base editing off-target profile appears favorable per preclinical data.
analysis_trace.key_risks: 1) Engraftment failure or poor durability; 2) Insufficient editing efficiency to reach 10% threshold; 3) Busulfan toxicity; 4) Immune response to edited cells; 5) Graft loss (observed in 3/19 prior lentiviral CGD patients).
analysis_trace.evidence_to_prediction: Preclinical study (Sci Transl Med 2024) demonstrated 70% correction efficiency for CYBB c.676C>T in HSPCs, with stable edited alleles post-transplant in mice. Prior lentiviral GT (Nat Med 2020) achieved 16-46% oxidase-positive neutrophils in 6/7 survivors at 12 months. Base editing avoids vector insertional risk and should achieve comparable or better engraftment with endogenous regulation.
analysis_trace.coverage_gaps: No published clinical results for this specific trial as of cutoff. Phase 1/2 design with small sample (n=15) limits precision. Long-term durability (>2 years) uncertain. No direct comparative data for base editing vs lentiviral GT in humans.

claims_supported: Trial design: Phase 1/2, single-arm, open-label
Target mutation: CYBB c.676C>T
Interventions: Base-edited HSPCs, busulfan conditioning, alemtuzumab, sirolimus
Primary endpoints: Safety and efficacy (>=10% oxidase-positive granulocytes)
Enrollment: 15 participants estimated
Status: RECRUITING
ABE8e-SpRY base editor achieved up to 70% correction of CYBB c.676C>T in HSPCs
Edited alleles persisted after transplantation into immunodeficient mice
Minimal off-target edits observed
IND-enabling studies support NCT06325709
Prior lentiviral gene therapy for X-CGD achieved 16-46% oxidase-positive neutrophils at 12 months in 6/7 survivors
Busulfan conditioning used in prior trials
Graft loss observed in 3/19 patients
Trial start date: April 2024
Follow-up schedule: months 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, then yearly to 5 years
Key assessments: AE evaluation, gp91phox protein, DNA sequencing for repair rates

trial_outcome_prediction.rationale: Preclinical data supports 70% editing efficiency for target mutation. Prior lentiviral GT achieved clinical efficacy in X-CGD. Base editing offers advantages: no vector insertional risk, endogenous gene regulation, no DSBs. Primary efficacy threshold (>=10% oxidase-positive granulocytes) appears achievable in majority of patients. Safety profile expected manageable with standard busulfan conditioning. Key risks: engraftment failure, insufficient editing durability, graft loss.
